content:
With the recent models, there has been a great uptick of large autoformalised projects.
However, I have not seen any discussion on how to actually use AI (cost) efficiently (and if there is, it might be time to come back to this again anyways). For example; I want to formalise a 110 page math paper, which does not need significant new theory not in mathlib. I am using Codex (since GPT 5.6 seems not far behind Fable but is much cheaper). I have also installed the mcp and lean4 skill.

But which version of GPT 5.6 is the best for this, i.e. Luna/Terra/Sol (Low/Medium/High)? Does this actually make a difference? If I want to formalise some chapter, is it best to first also state the lemmas (and make adversarial test against misoformilzations? Then, do I just tell the AI directly "Formalise the proof of Lemma 6.1" or is there a more efficient way? If I understand correctly, one should keep the context low. So for new chats to pick up what is the plan, is it advicable to have some .md file with the outline of th eproject which the AI should always read first, if yes, what is good to have there? Does it (still) make sense to use Aristotle for some stuff? Etc etc

So I would really love to hear from people who have used AI for large formalisation projects, what their actual workflow looks like to create these massive 300k LoC projects or whatever.

What’s your computer like ? Have you thought about using OpenLlama and some of the latest open models ?

It’s not a bad cost saving strategy to get one of the open agentic models to sweep through and do its best , before committing to pricey bleeding edge token cost ones.

Of course it’s topic dependent , but it’s likely to at least make some progress and perhaps save some of the frontier tokens.
I have ThinkPad E-Series and it can barely handle normal lake build, so I dont think doing anything locally is realistic :)

I also don't think there is a small model that can formalize on the level of frontier models. I'm saying this because even the best Chinese models (they are big) are not on par when it comes to Lean. It seems to me Lean coding must be in the pretraining, and it's not a priority for many model makers.

I have been using Claude Code with Opus on default/high setting. I have had a lot of luck with building minimal versions of a problem and then iteratively scaling patterns up. Building/testing a python version before rewriting it into Lean has been effective at making sure the basics (eg data/io) are correct. I have a bunch of CI checks that get triggered every time code gets pushed. ~200k+ LoC, but the skeleton is about ~10-15k.

Ralf Stephan said:

I also don't think there is a small model that can formalize on the level of frontier models. I'm saying this because even the best Chinese models (they are big) are not on par when it comes to Lean. It seems to me Lean coding must be in the pretraining, and it's not a priority for many model makers.

Yea but it would be ambitious to expect open models or small models to formalise at frontier level.

However the cost saving allows running for far longer and getting partial progress for frontier to take over (assuming you already happen to have a beefy computer) .

I have found local models can do a good amount of Lean personally, but agree certainly not close to frontier levels.

Leanstral, yes, but I meant generalist models. There is a new paper at https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.05632 and it comes down to differences in post-training, reasoning architecture/style, and how well the model handles the specific demands of heavy Lean 4 work.

So, either Opus, Gemini, GPT (maybe the new Grok), or a specialized model.

Just note that paper came out before Leanstral 1.5. Leanstral 1.5 is much better that Leanstral (1.0). And yes, it is not at Fable level, but for some workflows you don’t need that. Anyway, it was just a suggestion for the OP to try it and see if it helps.

Felix Pernegger said:

For example; I want to formalise a 110 page math paper, which does not need significant new theory not in mathlib. I am using Codex (since GPT 5.6 seems not far behind Fable but is much cheaper). I have also installed the mcp and lean4 skill.

Do you understand the material yourself? People typically get better results this way. Right now everything is an experimental science, you might be better off just trying things rather than asking. Probably a lot depends on the difficulty of the material, which you didn't specify. Don't let the machine set_option maxHeartbeats 10000000. Check that definitions are idiomatic. Did you consider instead making a roadmap and offloading the actual work to Tau Ceti?

One thing you could do if you really just want it formalized rather than having the experience of working on it yourself is hand it to Trellis (with your chatgpt subscription) : https://www.math.cmu.edu/~wes/trellis.php
(If you have issues doing this let me know and I will try to help out.)

To your question about models:
Sometimes in my tests I do actual randomized A/B testing of different settings or models. (honestly I should probably do this more than I do). I typically stop these tests earlier than I would if I was aiming for a level of statistical significance that I was planning to put in a methods section of a paper but in any case in part based on the tests I do use sol. (I have not run randomized tests of effort levels, though I probably should; I just use maximum effort all the time.)

1) Anchor it to well-written definitions and theorems. You want a top model for this, or write it yourself if capable. If there are theorems in places that are easy to define, that can help. Copying definitions is NOT easy, and may even be harder than proving the theorems.
2) If you are formalizing an existing it can better to keep LLM to from getting too creative, and going off on some dead-end. You need to have a prompt that tells it to actually try to follow the paper, or refer back to the paper when it thinks it is stuck.
3) LLMs can add axioms that aren't true, or prove theorems based on conditionals that are false or hard open problems. It works best if you can ground the LLM in calculating examples. It works best if the LLM is able to work out examples. This can help if you can give libraries that allow it to work out examples, but this will vary based on what area of math you are formalizing.
4) LLMs make mistakes all the time. You should tell the LLM to try find counterexamples before proving. Mis-stated theorems, before conditionals, problems with definitions, or even the text being wrong can lead it try proving things that just aren't true. If it can catch it early, it can then fix things.
5) There may be certain common techniques for proving things in your area of mathematics. It can help to have it think about building re-usable components for working with those things before just proving things. the LLM may not remember what infrastructure it built, so it can help to use memory, and prompt to remind it about what it already did.
6) The paper you are trying to formalize may depend on another paper, that also hasn't been formalized in mathlib. You should make sure to tell the AI to see when there is a hidden dependency. Then, it would help if you can actual find the paper, and give it to the LLM.
7) After your LLM claims to have proved, you want it then audit its work. You can use a auditor skill to have it print the axioms, and make sure everything looks right before moving on.
8) It is possible to use multiple agents once with a coordinator with worktrees if there are multiple things that aren't interdependent. It can speed up the process.
9) If you have a lot of computations, it can get slow to build after a while. Watch how long things are taking to build. Try to refactor the code, so that slows modules aren't constantly getting rebuilt. If your slow computation depends on something that is actively being worked on, it can cause it to keep getting rebuilt.
10) If the agent has tools to work out examples, it can help the agent do better. What this entails will depend on your area of math. I.E. if formalizing calculus, you want it to have an integration library to play with.
11) Certain LLM can get imposter syndrome, and not know their full capabilities. You also may need to tell them to be honest, or they will just make up more stuff. I've used "be ambitious and honest"
12) Sometimes LLMs will go off doing non-sense, thining they are partially finishing something. It could be good to have it assess it is doing speculative stuff which is conditional on something, which may or may not be true or easily provable. If you get the LLM to vary from tactical to strategic thinking at these intervals, it can help.
13) Fable is powerful, but it also has a tendency at times to claims to almost be done. I.E. just one more residuals to prove ..., and then run out of credits. Use fable if genuinely stuck, or maybe for initial definitions, but use sparingly unless you have unlimited money.
